articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M reserve fund sits untouched as commissioners debate drainage priorities
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a stormwater fee, the county has spent less than 12% of collected funds. Residents in Myrtle Grove and Warrington want to know why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $53.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but spent only $6.1 million on drainage projects
A $47.1 million reserve fund remains untouched while residents in flood-prone neighborhoods wait for promised infrastructure improvements
County commissioners remain split on whether to prioritize new construction or maintenance of existing drainage systems
articles.body:
The water rose fast on Doris Avenue last September. Linda Faulkner watched it climb the three concrete steps to her front door, then spill across the threshold into her living room. She had 40 minutes between the first drops of rain and two inches of standing water in her house.

"They told us the fee would fix this," Faulkner said. "That was three years ago."

Faulkner is one of roughly 142,000 Escambia County property owners who have paid a monthly stormwater fee since November 2023, when voters narrowly approved a referendum creating the dedicated funding stream. The fee—$7.50 per month for single-family homes, scaled up for commercial properties—was supposed to address decades of deferred drainage maintenance and flood mitigation.

The money came in. The projects did not.

According to county budget documents obtained by The Flightline, Escambia County has collected $53.2 million in stormwater fees over three fiscal years. It has spent $6.1 million. The remaining $47.1 million sits in a dedicated reserve account, earning interest while neighborhoods like Myrtle Grove and Warrington flood with increasing regularity.

Where the money went

The $6.1 million in expenditures breaks down into three categories: $2.8 million for staff salaries and administrative costs, $1.9 million for equipment purchases, and $1.4 million for actual construction projects.

Those construction projects include ditch maintenance in the Cantonment area, pipe replacement on Fairfield Drive, and a retention pond expansion near the Olive Road commercial corridor. All three projects were already in the planning stages before the stormwater fee passed.

County Public Works Director James Harmon defended the spending pace at a commission workshop last month.

"You can't rush infrastructure," Harmon said. "We needed staff. We needed equipment. We needed to build capacity before we could build projects."

The capacity-building argument has merit. Before 2023, the county had no dedicated stormwater division. Drainage issues were handled piecemeal by road crews when time allowed. The stormwater fee funded 14 new positions, including engineers, project managers and field technicians.

But three years in, the administrative phase shows no signs of ending.

The priority fight

Behind closed doors and occasionally in public meetings, county commissioners have split into two camps on how to spend the reserve fund.

Commissioners Jeff Bergosh and Doug Underhill have pushed for large-scale capital projects—new retention ponds, major culvert replacements, pump station construction. These projects carry price tags in the millions and timelines measured in years.

"We finally have the resources to do this right," Bergosh said at a June commission meeting. "I'm not interested in band-aids."

Commissioners Lumon May and Steven Barry have argued for faster deployment of funds toward maintenance and smaller repairs that could provide immediate relief to flooded neighborhoods. May represents District 3, which includes Myrtle Grove and Warrington—two of the county's most flood-prone areas.

"My constituents can't wait for a five-year capital plan," May said at the same meeting. "They need ditches cleaned now. They need pipes cleared now."

Commissioner Mike Kohler has positioned himself as a swing vote, expressing sympathy for both approaches without committing to either.

The result is paralysis. No comprehensive spending plan has reached a commission vote. Projects advance through the planning process, accumulate engineering studies, then stall.

What residents see

On Doris Avenue in Myrtle Grove, the drainage ditch that runs behind Faulkner's property hasn't been cleared in at least two years. Vegetation chokes the channel. Plastic bags and debris dam the flow at a culvert crossing.

"I've called. My neighbors have called," Faulkner said. "They say they're aware of the issue."

The pattern repeats across the county's low-lying neighborhoods. In Warrington, residents along Baars Street have documented standing water that persists for days after rain events. In Brownsville, a collapsed pipe under West Fairfield Drive has created a sinkhole that's been flagged with orange cones for eight months.

County records show 847 stormwater-related complaints filed in fiscal year 2025. Of those, 312 remain listed as "pending assessment." Another 289 are marked "assessed—awaiting funding allocation."

Only 246 complaints resulted in completed work.

The reserve question

County financial policy requires maintaining a reserve fund equal to at least 10% of annual operating expenses for each dedicated revenue stream. For the stormwater fund, that threshold is approximately $1.8 million.

The current $47.1 million reserve exceeds that requirement by a factor of 26.

Asked about the reserve level, County Administrator Wes Moreno pointed to uncertainty over future construction costs and potential federal matching funds.

"We want to be positioned to leverage opportunities," Moreno said. "If a federal grant requires a local match, we have it. If material costs spike, we're protected."

The federal matching fund argument refers to potential grants through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program and the EPA's Clean Water State Revolving Fund. The county has submitted applications for both programs, but neither has resulted in awards.

Meanwhile, the reserve fund continues to grow. Current projections show it reaching $62 million by the end of fiscal year 2027 if spending patterns hold.

What happens next

The county commission has scheduled a stormwater budget workshop for August 14. According to the agenda, commissioners will review a proposed five-year capital improvement plan and consider a resolution establishing spending priorities.

Public comment will be allowed. Faulkner plans to attend.

"I've got pictures from every flood since 2023," she said. "They can see exactly what their reserve fund looks like from my living room."

The workshop begins at 9 a.m. in the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building, 221 Palafox Place.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The last trailer park on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Camp Gulf has survived hurricanes, rezoning battles, and pressure from resort developers for six decades. Its 89 remaining tenants aren't sure they'll survive the next lease negotiation.
brief: Camp Gulf, the last remaining trailer park on Pensacola Beach, faces an uncertain future as its lease with Santa Rosa Island Authority expires in December 2027
The 89 tenants, many of them retirees who have lived there for decades, say they've received no guarantees about renewal terms or relocation assistance
Escambia County commissioners have fielded multiple unsolicited proposals from resort developers interested in the 12-acre beachfront property
articles.body:
The wind chimes on Lot 47 haven't stopped moving since 1987. That's when Gerald Hixon first backed his Airstream into the sandy patch of ground at Camp Gulf, sixty feet from the dune line. He was 34 then. He's 73 now.

"I've replaced the chimes three times," Hixon said on a Tuesday morning in June, sitting in a lawn chair beneath a sun-bleached awning. "Ivan got the first set. Dennis got the second. The salt air just ate the third."

Hixon has outlasted hurricanes. He's not sure he can outlast the next lease negotiation.

Camp Gulf sits on 12 acres of Santa Rosa Island Authority land at the western edge of Pensacola Beach, between Portofino towers and the national seashore boundary. Eighty-nine trailers and RVs occupy the site, most of them permanent residents who pay monthly lot rent of $650 plus utilities. It is the last trailer park on Pensacola Beach. The only one that survived the resort boom of the 1990s and 2000s.

Its lease expires December 31, 2027. Seventeen months from now.

A history of holding on

The park opened in 1962, when Pensacola Beach was still a fishing village with a few motels and a lot of sand. Families drove down from Montgomery and Birmingham to camp for a week. The trailers came later—seasonal at first, then year-round as retirees discovered they could live on the Gulf for less than the cost of a mobile home in town.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages all leases on the barrier island for Escambia County, has renewed Camp Gulf's ground lease four times since then. Each time, the terms got shorter. The current lease runs just 10 years.

"The authority has never said they want us gone," said Martha Creel, who has lived at Camp Gulf since 2003 and serves as an informal liaison between residents and SRIA staff. "But they've never said we can stay, either."

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio declined to comment on lease negotiations, citing ongoing discussions. Board Chair Brigette Brooks did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

What is clear from public records: Escambia County commissioners have received at least three unsolicited proposals since 2023 from developers interested in the Camp Gulf site. One proposal, from a Jacksonville-based hospitality group, envisioned a 200-room boutique hotel with "authentic Gulf Coast character." Another pitched a mixed-use development with vacation rentals and a marina.

None of the proposals have advanced to formal consideration. But none have been rejected, either.

"We're sitting on a gold mine"

The Camp Gulf property would appraise at roughly $28 million as vacant land, according to estimates from two commercial real estate brokers who spoke on background. Developed as a resort, it could generate annual lease payments to SRIA five to eight times higher than the current rate.

"Economically, there's no argument for keeping it as a trailer park," said one broker who has worked on Pensacola Beach deals. "The county's leaving millions on the table every year."

Current Camp Gulf tenants pay a combined annual ground rent of roughly $690,000 to SRIA, according to figures Creel compiled from resident surveys. A comparable hotel development would likely pay $3 million to $5 million annually.

Hixon knows the math. Everyone at Camp Gulf knows the math.

"We're sitting on a gold mine that we don't own," he said. "We've known that for thirty years. But there's supposed to be more to a community than extracting maximum value from every piece of dirt."

The hurricane question

Camp Gulf has taken direct hits from Hurricanes Erin in 1995, Opal in 1995, Ivan in 2004, Dennis in 2005, and Sally in 2020. Each storm thinned the herd. After Ivan, twenty-six units were condemned and removed. After Sally, eleven more.

The park's critics—and it has them, mostly on Pensacola Beach resident Facebook groups—argue that trailer parks are incompatible with barrier island resilience. Modern building codes require new construction to meet stringent wind-load and flood-elevation standards. Trailers don't.

"Every hurricane, we hold our breath wondering if Camp Gulf is going to scatter debris across the island," one Portofino resident wrote in a 2020 email to SRIA obtained through a public records request. "It's a liability and an eyesore."

Creel disputes this characterization. She notes that Camp Gulf residents are required to evacuate during mandatory orders—unlike hotel guests, who sometimes ignore warnings—and that the park has never generated significant debris outside its boundaries.

"Our trailers are tied down and inspected," she said. "We've been doing this longer than most of the condos have existed."

Who lives here

The 89 occupied lots at Camp Gulf house a population that skews older, whiter, and more working-class than Pensacola Beach as a whole. Many residents are retired military. Several are Vietnam veterans. A handful are service workers—bartenders, cleaners, fishing charter mates—who can't afford to live anywhere else on the island.

Donna Pfeiffer, 67, moved to Camp Gulf in 2019 after her husband died and she sold their house in Pace. Her lot rent and utilities run about $850 a month. A one-bedroom apartment in Gulf Breeze would cost twice that.

"I'm not beach trash," Pfeiffer said, using a term she's heard applied to Camp Gulf residents. "I worked for the school district for 31 years. I just want to live near the water while I still can."

If the lease isn't renewed, or if rents spike beyond affordability, Pfeiffer isn't sure where she'd go. Her trailer is worth maybe $15,000. Not enough to start over.

What happens next

The SRIA board is scheduled to discuss "long-term lease planning" at its August 14 meeting, according to a draft agenda reviewed by The Flightline. Camp Gulf is not specifically listed, but residents believe their fate will be part of the conversation.

Creel has organized a letter-writing campaign and plans to pack the meeting with tenants. She's also retained a Pensacola attorney, Michael Harrison, to represent resident interests in any formal negotiations.

"We're not asking for charity," Creel said. "We're asking for a fair deal and enough notice to plan our lives. That's it."

Harrison said he's advised residents to prepare for multiple scenarios, including the possibility that Camp Gulf closes entirely when the current lease expires.

"Hope for the best, prepare for the worst," he said. "That's all you can do when you're a tenant on land someone else controls."

Back on Lot 47, Hixon has started sorting through four decades of accumulated belongings. Just in case. He's not packing yet. But he's making lists.

"I always figured I'd die here," he said. "Now I figure I'll probably die somewhere else, thinking about here."

The wind chimes kept moving. The Gulf stayed where it's always been, sixty feet away, indifferent to leases and negotiations and the plans of men.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels 2027 schedule cuts two Gulf Coast shows as Navy eyes maintenance backlog
articles.dek: NAS Pensacola officials confirm the team will fly 62 demonstrations next season, down from 68. Pensacola Beach airshow remains on calendar, but Mobile and Biloxi dates eliminated.
brief: The Blue Angels will perform 62 demonstrations in 2027, down from 68 this season, as the Navy addresses a maintenance backlog on the team's F/A-18 Super Hornets.
Mobile's annual airshow and Biloxi's Keesler Air Force Base show have been cut from next year's schedule, though Pensacola Beach's July event remains confirmed.
Navy officials cite aging aircraft components and a nationwide shortage of aviation maintenance technicians as factors driving the reduced schedule.
articles.body:
The Blue Angels maintenance hangar at NAS Pensacola sat quiet Wednesday morning, its bay doors closed against the July heat. Inside, according to Navy officials, technicians were working through a parts replacement schedule that has forced the service to trim the flight demonstration team's 2027 calendar by nearly nine percent.

The Navy confirmed this week that the Blue Angels will fly 62 demonstrations next season, down from 68 scheduled for 2026. Two Gulf Coast shows—Mobile's annual airshow and the Keesler Air Force Base event in Biloxi—have been eliminated from the rotation.

Pensacola Beach's homecoming show, scheduled for July 10-11, 2027, remains on the calendar.

"This isn't about reducing our commitment to the communities we serve," said Cmdr. Alex Armatas, the Blue Angels' commanding officer and flight leader, in a statement released Tuesday. "This is about ensuring we can maintain the highest safety standards for our aircraft and our personnel."

Maintenance backlog driving cuts

Navy spokeswoman Lt. Cmdr. Patricia Kreuzberger told The Flightline that the reduced schedule stems from a convergence of factors affecting the team's fleet of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.

The Blue Angels transitioned from the legacy F/A-18 Hornet to the Super Hornet variant in 2021. Five years into that transition, certain airframe components are reaching the end of their initial service life and require replacement or refurbishment.

"We're dealing with scheduled maintenance intervals that were always part of the plan," Kreuzberger said by phone Wednesday. "What's changed is the timeline for getting parts and the availability of qualified technicians to install them."

She declined to specify which components required attention, citing operational security, but confirmed that the work would take place at the Blue Angels' home facility at NAS Pensacola and at the Naval Air Depot in Jacksonville.

The Navy has struggled in recent years to retain aviation maintenance personnel across the fleet. A Government Accountability Office report published in March found that the service was operating at 84 percent of required staffing levels for F/A-18 maintenance specialists.

Mobile, Biloxi shows cut

The Mobile Airshow, held annually at Mobile Downtown Airport, had featured the Blue Angels as its headline act for 11 consecutive years. Event organizers learned of the cancellation last week.

"We're disappointed, obviously," said Marcus Jernigan, executive director of the Mobile Airshow Foundation, reached by phone Wednesday. "But we understand the Navy has to make these decisions based on what's best for the program long-term."

Jernigan said organizers are in discussions with other military demonstration teams, including the Air Force Thunderbirds, about potentially filling the 2027 slot. He declined to characterize those conversations as negotiations.

The Keesler Air Force Base Thunder Over the Sound airshow, typically held in April, had featured the Blue Angels in alternating years. The 2027 event would have been a Blue Angels year under that rotation.

Keesler public affairs did not respond to requests for comment by publication time.

Pensacola show safe for now

The Pensacola Beach airshow, operated by the Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce in coordination with NAS Pensacola, will proceed as planned next July.

Chamber president Alison Westmoreland said she received confirmation from Navy officials on Monday that the homecoming show remained on the schedule.

"We never really had any doubt," Westmoreland said. "This is home. The Navy understands what this event means to our community and to the Blue Angels themselves."

The Pensacola Beach show drew an estimated 175,000 spectators across two days in 2025, according to chamber estimates. It generates an economic impact of approximately $22 million for Santa Rosa Island businesses, per a chamber-commissioned study.

Still, Westmoreland acknowledged that the reduced national schedule could affect the team's long-term presence in Pensacola.

"We're not taking anything for granted," she said. "We're going to keep working to make sure this event is the best it can be, every year."

Questions about future scheduling

The 2027 cuts mark the second consecutive year the Blue Angels have reduced their demonstration schedule. The team flew 70 shows in 2025 before trimming to 68 for 2026.

Navy officials have not indicated whether further reductions are planned for 2028 or beyond.

Rep. Matt Gaetz, whose district includes NAS Pensacola, issued a statement Wednesday expressing concern about the trend.

"The Blue Angels are ambassadors for naval aviation and a point of pride for Northwest Florida," Gaetz said. "I've asked the Navy to provide a detailed briefing on maintenance requirements and what resources are needed to return to a full demonstration schedule."

Kreuzberger, the Navy spokeswoman, said the service anticipates completing the current maintenance cycle by late 2027.

"Our goal is to return to a more robust schedule in future years," she said. "But we have to do this right. These aircraft and these pilots represent the very best of naval aviation. We won't compromise on safety or readiness."

The full 2027 Blue Angels schedule is expected to be published in October.
